Risk: Building something customers don't need or won't pay for
What it means: Development, hiring, and spend committed to a product before confirming real customers have the problem it solves and will pay to fix it - the cost lands later, as runway and months of team effort spent building toward a market that was never actually there.
Controls that usually help: Structured customer-discovery interviews before major build decisions; a tracked activation/retention signal reviewed on a cadence, not just at fundraising time; a named person accountable for challenging 'build it and they'll come' plans.

Risk: Premature scaling ahead of a confirmed repeatable model
What it means: Hiring aggressively or increasing spend before product-market fit and unit economics are actually confirmed, burning runway against an unproven model.
Controls that usually help: A stated, written definition of what 'repeatable' means for this business before scaling decisions are made; headcount and spend growth gated against that definition, not against available cash alone.

Risk: The business stalls when a founder or key leader is unavailable or in dispute
What it means: Major decisions and unique institutional knowledge sit with one or two people, undocumented - a founder dispute or departure can stall the business with no defined fallback.
Controls that usually help: Written decision-rights documentation for major calls (equity, hiring, spend thresholds); cross-training or documentation so no single departure is a single point of failure for the business itself, not just its infrastructure.

Risk: Slow to pivot away from a failing product, hire, or decision
What it means: Sunk-cost momentum or not actively gathering user feedback keeps a company committed to something that isn't working, burning runway and team morale on a course correction that gets more expensive, not less, the longer it's delayed.
Controls that usually help: A recurring, scheduled review of core product/growth assumptions against real usage data, not just internal conviction; an explicit owner for raising 'is this still working' rather than leaving it to consensus.

Risk: Revenue concentrated in a small number of customers
What it means: A small number of accounts driving most revenue means losing one is a material threat to the business, not just to a quarter's growth number.
Controls that usually help: Revenue-concentration tracked on a cadence (e.g. top-5-customer share of revenue); a stated threshold that triggers a deliberate diversification push rather than being noticed only after a cancellation.

Risk: Single point of failure in infrastructure or a key vendor
What it means: One vendor, one integration, one region, or one person that the business cannot operate without and has no fallback for - when it fails, the business stops outright for as long as that one thing is down, rather than just degrading.
Controls that usually help: An inventory of true single points of failure (infrastructure and people); a stated redundancy or fallback plan for each one rated Critical impact.

Risk: Technical debt that resists scaling
What it means: Early shortcuts compound into infrastructure that actively fights further growth, forcing an expensive rebuild at the worst possible time - under real load, not on a clean schedule.
Controls that usually help: A recurring engineering review that names debt explicitly (not just feature backlog); at least one identified rebuild trigger (a load or scale threshold) decided before it's hit under pressure.

Risk: Security gaps go unnoticed because no one owns security as a whole
What it means: Individual controls exist here and there - a backup, a password rule, maybe an incident plan - but nothing ties them together into one program a named person owns and can describe end to end. Gaps between the individual controls go unnoticed because no one is looking at the whole picture, and a buyer or auditor asking 'what is your security program' gets a list of fragments instead of an answer.
Controls that usually help: A single written information security policy, reviewed at least annually, that names every other control in this register as part of one program rather than leaving them to stand alone; a named owner for that program, even if it's the founder part-time rather than a dedicated hire.

Risk: A security incident goes unnoticed, or runs longer and costs more than it should
What it means: No documented process for detecting, responding to, and recovering from a security incident - the first real incident becomes the first time anyone follows a plan, live, which extends how long the incident runs and how much it costs to contain before anyone has practiced the response.
Controls that usually help: A written incident response plan, tested at least once via a tabletop exercise, not just filed away; monitoring or alerting for production systems, even lightweight, rather than relying on someone noticing.

Risk: Attackers exploit a known weakness that a patch already fixes
What it means: Third-party libraries and dependencies go unpatched because there is no routine process checking for known vulnerabilities - scanning happens never, or only after something breaks, by which point a known, already-patchable flaw has had an open window to actually be exploited, not just exist on paper.
Controls that usually help: Dependency/vulnerability scanning as a step in the normal build or deploy process, not a manual quarterly task; a stated expectation for how quickly a known-critical vulnerability gets patched.

Risk: Ungoverned use of AI tools by staff or within the product
What it means: Staff paste customer data, source code, or financial details into AI tools with no policy on which tools are approved or what can be shared with them, and AI-generated output gets used in decisions or code with no review step - so a wrong or fabricated answer reaches a customer or a codebase exactly like a correct one would.
Controls that usually help: A short written policy naming which AI tools are approved and what data may never be pasted into them; a human review step before AI-generated output reaches a customer, a decision, or production code, rather than trusting it directly.

Risk: Hiring or culture misalignment in the earliest hires
What it means: Early team members set the company's cultural DNA - values or working-style mismatches in the first hires compound faster than most market pressure, surfacing later as attrition, slower execution, or a culture the founders no longer recognize.
Controls that usually help: A stated set of values or working norms used explicitly in early hiring decisions, not just skills screening; a defined process for addressing an early misalignment quickly rather than hoping it resolves itself.

Risk: A former employee, contractor or outgrown role still has access to systems or customer data
What it means: Access to production systems and customer data isn't reviewed on a cadence or revoked promptly when someone leaves or changes roles, leaving a former employee or an outgrown role with a live path into customer data or production systems that no one is watching.
Controls that usually help: A recurring (at least quarterly) review of who has access to what; access revocation as a required, checked step of any offboarding.

Risk: Cash flow mismanagement hidden by burn-rate tunnel vision
What it means: Knowing the headline burn rate isn't the same as understanding what's actually driving it - operational inefficiencies can quietly drain runway well before the topline number looks alarming.
Controls that usually help: A regular breakdown of burn by driver, not just a single monthly total; a named runway trigger (e.g. months remaining) that forces a real conversation, decided before it's reached.

Risk: The company breaks a rule that applies to it without knowing
What it means: Regulatory requirements that plainly apply to the business are neither tracked nor documented - non-compliance is only discovered when a regulator, auditor, or customer flags it externally, and by then the exposure is fines, a forced remediation timeline, or a stalled deal, not just the cost the program would have taken to build.
Controls that usually help: An inventory of the regulatory regimes that actually apply to this business, reviewed at least annually; a named owner for regulatory compliance, even if it's the founder, rather than no owner at all.

Risk: Buyers can't see how the company protects them, and trust suffers
What it means: Nothing public states the company's actual security and operational posture - a security-conscious buyer has no way to evaluate the company without a manual, ad hoc request, and silence reads the same as having something to hide.
Controls that usually help: A public page stating real operational posture (uptime, backup cadence, incident history) honestly, including gaps, rather than only marketing claims; the page kept current enough that it doesn't quietly go stale.

Risk: Slow or poorly handled communication makes a security incident worse
What it means: There's no prepared plan for what gets communicated, to whom, and how fast, if a real security incident is confirmed - improvising that communication in the moment tends to make the incident's fallout worse than the incident itself.
Controls that usually help: A stated customer-notification commitment (a time window, e.g. 72 hours) agreed before it's ever needed; a named person responsible for external communication during an incident, decided in advance rather than during the event.

Risk: Runway shorter than the next fundraise will take
What it means: The cash on hand runs out before a new round can realistically close. Fundraising takes months, and a company that starts late negotiates from weakness or runs out of options altogether.
Controls that usually help: A runway forecast refreshed monthly, with the date fundraising must begin written down; a burn plan tied to the milestones that unlock the next round; agreed cost cuts ready to trigger if a raise slips; bridge options identified in advance.

Risk: Investors and the board lose confidence because they hear too little, too late
What it means: Investors and directors hear about the business irregularly and without consistent numbers. Trust erodes, help arrives late, and the next raise starts from a position of doubt.
Controls that usually help: A monthly investor update on a fixed date covering cash, runway, five to seven agreed metrics, wins and problems; a quarterly board pack with the risk register summary, sent ahead of the meeting; minutes and decisions recorded.

Risk: Nobody can say with confidence what the business earned, and diligence stalls
What it means: The accounts are kept on a cash basis or caught up in bursts, so nobody can say with confidence what the business earned last month. Due diligence stalls while months of records are rebuilt under pressure.
Controls that usually help: A monthly close finished within 10-15 working days; accrual accounting with a written revenue-recognition policy; bank and card accounts reconciled every month; a close checklist signed off by someone other than the preparer.

Risk: One person can move money from start to finish
What it means: The same person can set up a payee, approve a payment and reconcile the bank. Nobody else would notice a mistake or a theft until it had been happening for months.
Controls that usually help: Segregation of duties: separate people set up payees, approve payments and reconcile the bank; dual approval above a set amount; a monthly review of payments by a founder or director; a confidential route for staff to report concerns.

Risk: The company does not clearly own its intellectual property
What it means: Code, designs or content were created by founders before incorporation, or by contractors, without being assigned to the company. A buyer's or investor's lawyers will find it, and it can stop a deal.
Controls that usually help: Signed IP assignment agreements from every founder, employee and contractor; an assignment clause in every contractor template; a register of key IP (code, trademarks, domains) and who created it; trademark filings in core markets.

Risk: Cap table and equity promises not fully documented
What it means: Share issues, options, SAFEs, notes or verbal equity promises are not all recorded and reconciled. Ownership becomes uncertain exactly when an investor or buyer needs it to be clear.
Controls that usually help: A single cap table system reconciled to signed documents; board approval recorded for every issue and grant; vesting terms in writing; a quarterly reconciliation by counsel or finance.

Risk: Enterprise deals stall on security and compliance reviews
What it means: Large customers send security questionnaires and ask for evidence the company cannot readily produce. Deals slow or stop in procurement, and the sales team spends days on each review.
Controls that usually help: A maintained library of security answers and evidence; written policies mapped to SOC 2 or ISO 27001 control areas; a trust page and subprocessor list; a decision on when an independent report is worth pursuing, based on the deal pipeline.

Risk: Commitments made to customers in contracts aren't tracked
What it means: Contracts promise uptime, response times, security measures, data handling or notice periods that nobody is monitoring. A breach is discovered by the customer rather than the company.
Controls that usually help: A contract register listing each customer's commitments, renewal and notice dates; standard terms with a defined approval route for exceptions; operations sign-off before non-standard commitments are agreed.

Risk: Personal data is used or kept in a way that breaks data protection law
What it means: The company collects and uses personal data without knowing exactly what it holds, why, or which suppliers process it. Data protection laws apply regardless of company size.
Controls that usually help: A record of processing activities; data processing agreements with every supplier that handles personal data; a privacy notice that matches practice; a process for access and deletion requests; privacy reviews for new features.

Risk: A serious disruption stops the company serving customers for longer than they will tolerate
What it means: If a key system, office, supplier or person became unavailable for a week, there is no agreed way to keep serving customers. Backups exist but have never been restored.
Controls that usually help: A business continuity plan naming critical services and the maximum tolerable downtime for each; backups with a scheduled restore test; a recovery runbook; a tabletop exercise each year.

Risk: Insurance doesn't match what investors, contracts and the business need
What it means: Cover was bought once, or not at all. Investors expect directors' cover, enterprise contracts demand cyber and professional liability at set limits, and a gap surfaces at closing or during a claim.
Controls that usually help: An annual insurance review against the business's risks, investor requirements and signed contracts; directors and officers, cyber and professional liability cover where relevant; a register of insurance obligations in customer contracts.

Risk: Tax obligations triggered by growth go unnoticed
What it means: Selling into new states or countries creates sales tax, VAT or digital services tax obligations once thresholds are crossed. Nobody is watching the thresholds, and the liability builds quietly.
Controls that usually help: A quarterly review of sales by jurisdiction against registration thresholds; advice on the product's taxability in core markets; tax collection built into billing; registrations filed before thresholds are crossed.

Risk: Income and costs in different currencies with no plan for rate moves
What it means: The business earns in one currency and pays in another. A sharp exchange-rate move can wipe out margin or shorten runway without anything changing in the business itself.
Controls that usually help: A currency exposure view showing income, costs and cash by currency; natural hedging by matching income and costs where possible; a policy on how much cash to hold in each currency; pricing reviewed after large rate moves.

Risk: Misconduct stays hidden until it becomes public, legal or expensive
What it means: There is no code of conduct and no confidential route to report wrongdoing. Problems stay hidden until they become public, legal or expensive.
Controls that usually help: A short code of conduct every employee acknowledges; a confidential or anonymous reporting channel; a named person to investigate reports promptly; a written no-retaliation policy.

Risk: Critical processes live in people's heads
What it means: How the business actually runs - billing, onboarding, releases, month end - is known to the people who do it and written down nowhere. Growth, holidays and departures turn into errors and slowdowns.
Controls that usually help: Written procedures for critical and repeated processes, each with an owner and a review date; onboarding that uses them; handover and knowledge transfer built into offboarding; recurring manual work reviewed for automation.
